props.title: Dodsworth

sections.content: Dodsworth (1936) stands as one of Hollywood's most sophisticated examinations of a failing marriage, directed with remarkable restraint by William Wyler. The film follows Sam Dodsworth, a retired auto magnate, and his wife Fran as they travel through Europe, watching their relationship crumble with devastating precision. Unlike the melodramas of its era, Dodsworth's power comes from its mature, nuanced approach to middle-aged romance and identity - themes that would later influence works like Brief Encounter (1945) and The Apartment (1960).

sections.content: Walter Huston's performance as Sam Dodsworth set new standards for portraying complex middle-aged characters in Hollywood. His subtle portrayal influenced later performances like Fredric March in The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) and Spencer Tracy in Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967). Ruth Chatterton's Fran Dodsworth presents an unusually complex female character for the 1930s - a woman fighting against aging and seeking fulfillment beyond her prescribed social role.

The film's European settings allowed Wyler to explore themes of American identity abroad, predating similar explorations in films like An American in Paris (1951) and Roman Holiday (1953). Sidney Howard's adaptation of Sinclair Lewis's novel maintains the book's sharp social commentary while adding layers of visual sophistication that would influence the "theater of manners" films of the 1940s. sections.content: Cinematographer Rudolph Maté's work on Dodsworth pioneered the deep-focus techniques that would later become associated with Citizen Kane (1941). The film's handling of divorce and marital discord was revolutionary for its time, paving the way for adult dramas like The Heiress (1949) and Sunset Boulevard (1950). Wyler's decision to shoot in long takes, allowing scenes to play out naturally, influenced directors from Orson Welles to Martin Scorsese.
